lines: This is minidb, a small database engine we built from scratch in TypeScript.
In three minutes you will know how it stores rows, finds them, and survives a power cut.
A database is a very careful filing clerk with three jobs.
Store rows. Find them fast, without reading everything.
And never lose anything, even if the power goes out in the middle of a write.
Everything starts with pages. The whole database is one file, cut into four kilobyte blocks.
Each page is like a sheet of paper with a small index in its top margin: item two starts at byte thirty-eight ten.
Rows are written from the bottom up, the index grows from the top down, and the gap in the middle is free space.
A table is a chain of pages. A row's address is its page number and its slot number.
To find a row by id without reading everything, we keep a B plus tree: a sorted tree of pages, copied from Postgres.
Looking up id four takes two hops. Root says go right. The leaf says: page seven, slot three.
Reading the disk is slow, so we keep five hundred twelve pages in memory.
When you insert a row, only the in-memory copies of page seven and page nine change. We call them dirty.
The disk is untouched. If the power went out now, the row would vanish, and that is correct: you were never told it was saved.
Here is the trick that makes it safe. Before touching the real file, commit copies every dirty page into a second file, the write-ahead log.
Then it appends a COMMIT marker, then calls fsync, which waits until the bytes are physically on the disk.
Only then do you get your confirmation. The data file is still old, and that does not matter.
Now pull the plug. On restart, minidb reads the log. Every entry carries a checksum.
It replays everything up to the last COMMIT marker into the data file, and throws the torn tail away.
A confirmed change can never be lost. A half-written one can never survive.
On top of all that sits SQL. Your text becomes tokens, then a tree.
The binder checks types: comparing an integer column to text is an error, just like Postgres.
The planner decides: id has an index, so use it. The executor pulls rows one at a time through a chain of small nodes.
Seven layers, each talking only to the one below: pages, the log, the page cache, tables and indexes, the catalog, the SQL front end, and the front door.
About four thousand lines of TypeScript and thirty-four tests, including a child process that gets killed mid-write six times.
The code, the research notes, and an interactive explainer are in the repo.
Open the REPL and type EXPLAIN to watch the planner think.
